prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We present an x-ray spectromicroscopic investigation of single-crystalline magnetic FeMn/Co bilayers on Cu(001), using X-ray magnetic circular (XMCD) and linear (XMLD) dichroism at the Co and Fe L3 absorption edges in combination with photoelectron emission microscopy (PEEM). Using the magnetic coupling between the ferromagnetic Co layer and the antiferromagnetic FeMn layer we are able to produce magnetic domains with two different crystallographic orientations of the magnetic easy axis within the same sample at the same time. We find a huge difference in the XMLD contrast between the two types of magnetic domains, which we discuss in terms of intrinsic magneto-crystalline anisotropy of XMLD of the Co layer. We also demonstrate that due to the high sensitivity of the method, the small number of induced ferromagnetic Fe moments at the FeMn-Co interface is sufficient to obtain magnetic contrast from XMLD in a metallic system.

outputs.L1: We present an X-ray spectromicroscopic investigation of single-crystalline magnetic FeMn/Co bilayers on Cu(001), employing X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) and X-ray magnetic linear dichroism (XMLD) at the Co and Fe L₃ absorption edges in combination with photoelectron emission microscopy (PEEM). By exploiting the magnetic coupling between the ferromagnetic Co layer and the antiferromagnetic FeMn layer, we are able to generate, within the same sample and simultaneously, magnetic domains with two distinct crystallographic orientations of the magnetic easy axis. We observe a pronounced difference in XMLD contrast between these two types of magnetic domains, which we discuss in terms of the intrinsic magnetocrystalline anisotropy of XMLD in the Co layer. We further demonstrate that, owing to the high sensitivity of the method, the small number of induced ferromagnetic Fe moments at the FeMn/Co interface is sufficient to produce magnetic contrast from XMLD in a metallic system.
outputs.L2: We report an X-ray spectromicroscopy study of single-crystal magnetic FeMn/Co bilayers grown on Cu(001). The measurements combine photoelectron emission microscopy (PEEM) with X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) and X-ray magnetic linear dichroism (XMLD) recorded at the Co and Fe L3 absorption edges. By exploiting the magnetic interaction between the ferromagnetic Co film and the antiferromagnetic FeMn film, we can create, within one sample and simultaneously, magnetic domains whose easy magnetization axes have two distinct crystallographic orientations. We observe a very large variation in XMLD contrast between these two domain types, which we interpret as arising from the intrinsic magnetocrystalline anisotropy of the XMLD signal in the Co layer. In addition, we show that the technique is sensitive enough that even the limited population of ferromagnetic Fe moments induced at the FeMn/Co interface can generate detectable XMLD magnetic contrast in a metallic system.

The study investigates single-crystalline magnetic FeMn/Co bilayers grown on Cu(001) using a combination of x-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD), x-ray magnetic linear dichroism (XMLD), and photoemission electron microscopy (PEEM). These element-sensitive magnetic imaging techniques allow the researchers to study both the ferromagnetic Co layer and the antiferromagnetic FeMn layer with spatial resolution, making it possible to correlate domain structures and magnetic anisotropies within the same sample.

A central aspect of the work is the magnetic coupling between the ferromagnetic cobalt layer and the antiferromagnetic iron-manganese layer. This coupling produces magnetic domains that can exhibit two different crystallographic easy-axis orientations in a single sample. As a result, the system provides a useful platform for directly comparing the magnetic response of domains with different orientations under otherwise identical experimental conditions.

Using XMLD-PEEM imaging, the researchers observe a pronounced difference in XMLD contrast between the two types of magnetic domains. This contrast variation indicates that the XMLD signal is not determined only by the relative orientation between the x-ray polarization and the local magnetic axis, but is also strongly influenced by the crystallographic direction along which the magnetization lies.

The large XMLD contrast difference is attributed to the intrinsic magneto-crystalline anisotropy of the Co layer. In other words, the XMLD response depends on the relationship between the Co magnetic moments and the crystal lattice. Domains aligned along different crystallographic easy axes therefore produce different XMLD intensities, even when they are part of the same continuous film. This demonstrates that XMLD can provide direct information about magneto-crystalline effects in ferromagnetic thin films.

The study also shows that the experimental approach is highly sensitive. In particular, it is capable of detecting XMLD magnetic contrast arising from only a small number of ferromagnetic Fe moments induced at the FeMn-Co interface. This sensitivity highlights the usefulness of XMCD, XMLD, and PEEM for probing interfacial magnetism in layered magnetic systems, where only a very small fraction of atoms may contribute to the measured magnetic signal.
outputs.L4:
X-ray spectromicroscopy was used to investigate the magnetic domain structure of single-crystalline FeMn/Co bilayers grown on Cu(001). By combining x-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) and x-ray magnetic linear dichroism (XMLD) with photoemission electron microscopy (PEEM), the experiment provided element-specific, spatially resolved information about the magnetic order in both the ferromagnetic Co layer and the antiferromagnetic FeMn layer. This approach made it possible to image magnetic domains directly and to distinguish contributions from different magnetic mechanisms.

A key feature of the samples was the magnetic coupling between Co and FeMn. This coupling allowed domains with different crystallographic easy-axis orientations to be stabilized within the same specimen. As a result, the sample served as an internal comparison system: different domain types could be studied under identical experimental conditions, eliminating uncertainties that might arise from comparing separate samples.

The measurements revealed a pronounced difference in XMLD contrast between the different domain types. This contrast variation could not be explained solely by geometrical effects or by changes in domain orientation relative to the x-ray polarization. Instead, it was attributed to an intrinsic magnetocrystalline anisotropy of the Co layer. In other words, the XMLD signal depended strongly on the crystallographic direction of the magnetic easy axis, demonstrating that XMLD in Co is sensitive not only to the spin direction but also to the underlying crystal symmetry and anisotropic electronic structure.

In addition to imaging the Co domains, the study showed that XMLD-PEEM is sensitive enough to detect magnetic contrast associated with very small induced Fe moments at the metallic FeMn–Co interface. Although FeMn is antiferromagnetic in bulk form, the proximity to the ferromagnetic Co layer can induce uncompensated or spin-polarized Fe moments at the interface. The observation of XMLD contrast from these interfacial Fe moments demonstrates the high sensitivity of the technique to buried or interface-related magnetic phenomena, even when the magnetic signal is weak.

Overall, the work highlights the power of combining XMCD, XMLD, and PEEM for studying complex magnetic heterostructures with element specificity and high spatial resolution. The results provide insight into the role of crystallographic anisotropy in XMLD contrast and show that interfacial magnetic moments in exchange-coupled antiferromagnet/ferromagnet systems can be detected directly. Such findings are important for understanding exchange coupling, magnetic anisotropy, and domain formation in layered magnetic materials.
outputs.L5:
FeMn alloys are widely studied antiferromagnetic materials with important applications in spintronics, magnetic multilayers, and exchange-bias systems. Because FeMn typically exhibits antiferromagnetic order rather than a large net magnetic moment, conventional magnetometry can be insufficient for understanding its microscopic magnetic structure. Element-specific synchrotron techniques such as X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) and X-ray magnetic linear dichroism (XMLD) are therefore especially valuable for investigating FeMn-based systems.

XMCD measures the difference in X-ray absorption for left- and right-circularly polarized light. It is sensitive to the net magnetic moment of a selected element, making it useful for detecting uncompensated spins or induced magnetic moments in FeMn. For example, at an FeMn/ferromagnet interface, XMCD can reveal whether Fe or Mn atoms acquire a small ferromagnetic component due to exchange coupling. Since the method is element-specific, measurements at the Fe and Mn absorption edges can distinguish the separate magnetic contributions of each element.

XMLD, in contrast, uses linearly polarized X-rays and is sensitive to the orientation of magnetic moments relative to the polarization direction. This makes XMLD particularly powerful for studying antiferromagnets such as FeMn, where the total magnetization may vanish even though the material has a well-defined spin axis. XMLD can provide information about the antiferromagnetic domain structure, spin orientation, and magnetic anisotropy. In FeMn thin films, XMLD is often used to probe how the antiferromagnetic order is influenced by strain, film thickness, temperature, and coupling to adjacent ferromagnetic layers.

Together, XMCD and XMLD offer complementary information. XMCD detects net or uncompensated magnetic moments, while XMLD probes antiferromagnetic order. In FeMn systems, this combination is particularly useful for studying exchange bias, interfacial spin structures, and the coupling between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic layers. As a result, XMCD and XMLD have become essential tools for understanding the microscopic magnetic behavior of FeMn and for optimizing its role in advanced magnetic devices.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize research findings on XMLD contrast differences in Co magnetic domains coupled to FeMn, including the role of crystallographic easy-axis orientation and interfacial induced ferromagnetic Fe moments.
counterfactuals.output:
Research on XMLD imaging of Co domains exchange-coupled to FeMn shows that the observed contrast is not simply a generic “magnetic-domain” contrast, but depends strongly on both crystallography and interface magnetism.

Key findings:

- **XMLD is sensitive to magnetization-axis orientation, not magnetization polarity.**  
  In Co, XMLD contrast mainly distinguishes domains whose magnetization lies along different in-plane axes, e.g. 90° domains. Opposite 180° domains should give essentially the same XMLD signal because XMLD is even in the magnetization direction.

- **The crystallographic easy-axis direction matters.**  
  Co domains coupled to FeMn often align along crystallographic easy axes imposed by the Co film and/or by exchange coupling to the antiferromagnetic FeMn. Because XMLD spectra depend on the angle between the magnetic axis, the x-ray polarization, and the crystal axes, domains magnetized along different easy axes can show different XMLD intensity or even different spectral line shapes. Thus, contrast differences can arise from whether the Co moment lies along one crystalline easy axis versus another, not only from domain orientation relative to the x-ray beam.

- **Exchange coupling to FeMn modifies the Co domain pattern.**  
  The antiferromagnetic FeMn layer can pin or bias the Co magnetization through interfacial exchange. This coupling can favor certain Co easy-axis orientations and stabilize domain configurations that reflect the underlying AF order or the interfacial exchange-bias direction.

- **Fe-edge contrast is not always purely antiferromagnetic FeMn XMLD.**  
  At the Co/FeMn interface, some Fe moments in FeMn can acquire an induced ferromagnetic component due to direct coupling with Co. These uncompensated or interfacially polarized Fe moments align with the Co magnetization.

- **Interfacial ferromagnetic Fe moments can mimic or modify XMLD contrast.**  
  Because the induced Fe moments follow the Co domains, Fe \(L\)-edge images may show domain contrast correlated with the Co domain structure. Part of the Fe contrast may therefore come from ferromagnetically polarized interfacial Fe rather than from the bulk antiferromagnetic spin axis of FeMn. This is especially important when interpreting XMLD-PEEM data, since the probing depth is surface/interface sensitive.

Overall, the studies show that XMLD contrast in Co/FeMn systems is governed by a combination of:  
1. the orientation of Co magnetization relative to crystallographic easy axes and x-ray polarization,  
2. exchange coupling between Co and antiferromagnetic FeMn, and  
3. ferromagnetically induced Fe moments at the interface.  

Therefore, XMLD contrast differences cannot be interpreted solely as simple maps of Co or FeMn domain polarity; they must be analyzed with the crystallographic anisotropy and interfacial magnetic polarization in mind.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a technical abstract about using x-ray magnetic circular and linear dichroism microscopy to study single-crystal FeMn/Co bilayers, highlighting domain engineering, anisotropic XMLD contrast, and sensitivity in metallic systems.
counterfactuals.output:
X-ray magnetic circular and linear dichroism microscopy (XMCD/XMLD-PEEM or scanning soft x-ray microscopy) provides an element-specific probe of ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic order in exchange-coupled metallic heterostructures. Here, we describe its application to single-crystal FeMn/Co bilayers as a model system for imaging and engineering interfacial magnetic domains. XMCD at the Co absorption edges directly images the ferromagnetic Co domain configuration, while XMLD at the Fe and Mn edges reveals the orientation of antiferromagnetic spin axes in the FeMn layer through its polarization-dependent absorption. By combining circular and linear dichroic contrast under controlled magnetic-field and thermal histories, the coupling between Co ferromagnetic domains and FeMn antiferromagnetic domains can be spatially resolved.

The single-crystal nature of the bilayers enables deterministic domain engineering through crystallographic anisotropy, exchange coupling, and patterned or field-induced preparation protocols. In particular, XMLD contrast is strongly anisotropic: its magnitude and sign depend on the relative orientation between the x-ray electric-field vector, the antiferromagnetic spin axis, and the crystal axes. This anisotropy permits separation of distinct antiferromagnetic domain variants that may be indistinguishable by topography or conventional magnetometry, but it also requires careful control of sample azimuth and polarization geometry for quantitative interpretation.

Despite the limited x-ray penetration depth and the generally weak dichroic response of metallic antiferromagnets compared with oxides, soft x-ray dichroism microscopy remains sufficiently sensitive to detect buried or ultrathin FeMn spin textures through element-specific absorption contrast. The technique therefore provides a powerful route to correlate ferromagnetic domain patterns, antiferromagnetic domain selection, and exchange-bias behavior in metallic bilayers, enabling microscopic insight into domain-state control in spintronic materials.
